messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Object Throwing: Throwing objects, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus is a forty-two-year-old ship captain who has spent his entire adult life on the water, commanding crews through storms and tight schedules with a steady hand. He came to therapy at the insistence of his wife, who told him she could not watch him disappear any further. He sat in the chair with his arms crossed, scanning the room before he sat down, then chose the seat with his back to the wall. He did not call it anything. He simply said he felt better that way.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, on a cargo vessel out of a Gulf port. Marcus had been piloting the ship through a narrow channel when a deckhand, during a routine line-handling evolution, hurled a heavy mooring line across the deck in frustration. The line struck a piece of loose equipment, which skidded and struck a pressurized cylinder. The cylinder ruptured with a sound Marcus later described as the world splitting open—a bang so loud and percussive that he felt it in his teeth. The explosion killed two men instantly and severely burned a third. Marcus was thrown against the console and suffered a concussion, but he was the one who had to give orders for the emergency response, who had to radio for help, who had to stand on the bridge while the bodies were recovered. He still remembers the sight of the uniforms—Coast Guard and port authority—swarming the deck afterward, their crisp blue fabric soaked with seawater and blood.

In the months that followed, Marcus did not talk about it. He told himself he was fine, that he had handled worse, that a captain does not fall apart. But his body began to make decisions his mind would not acknowledge. He started dropping responsibilities. He took a sudden leave of absence from his command, citing exhaustion, and then quietly resigned from the shipping company altogether. He told his wife he needed a break, but the truth was that he could not bring himself to step onto a vessel again. The thought of being on the water, of hearing a line slap the deck or a hatch slam shut, made his chest tighten until he could not breathe. He had come to believe that if he let himself think about that day—really think about it, replay the bang and the sight of the uniforms and the sound of the cylinder—he would not be able to handle it. He would lose control entirely. So he kept the memory locked away, and he filled the space around it with other things.

He started gambling. At first it was just online poker late at night, a way to distract himself when the images crept in. Then it became a daily ritual, then an expensive one. He lost thousands of dollars, but the risk, the focus, the rush of the next hand—it kept the explosion at bay. He told himself it was just a hobby, but his wife found the credit card statements and the arguments began. He did not tell her about the other changes. He had become vigilant in a way that exhausted him. Every time he walked into a store or a restaurant, he scanned for exits, for people who looked threatening, for anyone wearing a uniform. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely because he could not assess the danger in advance. He could not trust that a stranger would not throw something, that a loud noise would not come from somewhere he could not see. He had stopped going to his son’s baseball games because the crowd was too unpredictable, too many people moving too fast. He had come to believe that he could not rely on other people—not his crew, not the port authorities, not the company that had paid off the families of the dead men without ever holding anyone accountable. The deckhand who threw the line was never charged. The investigation was quietly closed. Marcus was certain that if the world could let that happen, then no one was looking out for him, and he had to be the one watching.

Sleep became a battleground. He would lie awake for hours, his ears straining for any sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, his wife rolling over in bed. He kept his eyes open in the dark, listening, because he was sure that if he let himself fall asleep, he would not be alert enough to survive whatever came next. He had not had a full night’s rest in over a year.

What finally brought him to therapy was not the insomnia or the gambling or the isolation. It was the morning his wife told him she was thinking of leaving. She said she did not know who he was anymore. Marcus sat in the therapist’s office and said, very quietly, that he was afraid she was right. He did not know if he could get back to who he used to be. But he was even more afraid that if he started talking about what happened, he would never stop falling.
